title: Greatest common factor
competency: Find the GCF of two or more natural numbers and use it to solve problems.

keywords.def: A number that divides another number exactly.
A number that divides two numbers exactly.
Writing a number as a product of primes: 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3.

en.text: A common factor divides both numbers exactly. The greatest common factor is the largest one. To find it fast, write each number as a product of primes and multiply only the primes they share.

am.text: የጋራ አካፋይ ሁለቱንም ቁጥሮች ያለ ቀሪ ይካፍላል። ትልቁ የጋራ አካፋይ ከነዚህ ውስጥ ትልቁ ነው። በፍጥነት ለማግኘት እያንዳንዱን ቁጥር በብቸኛ ቁጥሮች ውጤት ጻፍና የሚጋሯቸውን ብቻ አባዛ።

screens.title: Cover the board
screens.text: A teacher wants to cover a whiteboard, 50 cm long and 20 cm wide, with square papers. All squares are the same size. No gaps, no overlaps.
screens.ask: What is the biggest square she can use? Take a guess.
screens.after:
Now test your guess on the board.
A square fits if a whole number of squares fits along 50 cm and along 20 cm.
10 cm works: 5 squares along, 2 squares down. 20 cm does not divide 50.

screens.title: Test some sizes
screens.text: Before you tap a size, say if it will fit. Then see. Red strips are gaps.

screens.title: What do the sizes that fit share?
screens.text: Common factors: the sizes that fit exactly are 1, 2, 5 and 10 cm. What do they share?
opts: Each one is an even number
screens.why:
A square fits only if a whole number fits along each edge.
5 cm: 50 ÷ 5 = 10 and 20 ÷ 5 = 4. Both whole, so it fits.
4 cm: 20 ÷ 4 = 5, but 50 ÷ 4 = 12.5. It does not fit.
So each size that fits divides both 50 and 20.
(Being even is not enough: 4 is even and fails.)
screens.clue: Try 5 cm. Is 50 ÷ 5 a whole number? Is 20 ÷ 5?

screens.title: Factors they share
defs: A number that divides two numbers exactly. 1, 2, 5 and 10 are common factors of 50 and 20.
The largest common factor. We write GCF(50, 20) = 10.

screens.title: Find the common factors
screens.text: Common factors of 12 and 18: tap every number that divides both 12 and 18 exactly.
screens.why:
Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.
Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18.
In both lists: 1, 2, 3, 6.
4 and 12 do not divide 18. 9 and 18 do not divide 12.
The largest is 6, so GCF(12, 18) = 6.
screens.clue: Test each number: does it divide 12 and also 18?

screens.title: Factor tree for 36
screens.intro: First write 36 as primes. Tap ▶ for each split.

screens.title: Factor tree for 56
screens.intro: Now 56. Which primes does it share with 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3?

screens.title: A faster way for big numbers
screens.text: Listing every factor gets slow. Prime factors give the GCF quickly. Example: 36 and 56.
steps: Write each number as primes: 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 and 56 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 7.
Two 2s appear in both numbers. Put them in the overlap.
Put the rest in their own circle: 3 and 3 for 36, then 2 and 7 for 56.

screens.title: Use the overlap
screens.why:
24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 54 = 2 × 3 × 3 × 3.
Shared primes: one 2 (54 has only one 2) and one 3 (24 has only one 3).
Multiply the shared primes: 2 × 3 = 6.
Check: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 and 54 ÷ 6 = 9, and 4 and 9 share no factor.
So GCF(24, 54) = 6.
screens.clue: Find the primes that appear in both lists, then multiply only those.
screens.worked: Shared primes: one 2 and one 3. Multiply them: 2 × 3 = 6. So GCF(24, 54) = 6.

screens.title: True or false?
screens.text: GCF of two primes: two different prime numbers, such as 7 and 11, always have GCF 1.
screens.why:
The factors of 7 are 1 and 7.
The factors of 11 are 1 and 11.
The only common factor is 1.
This happens for any two different primes, so GCF = 1. True.
screens.clue: Write all the factors of 7, then all the factors of 11.

screens.title: Traffic-safety teams
screens.text: A school has 14 girls and 21 boys for traffic-safety duty. Every team gets the same number of girls and the same number of boys, and everyone is in a team.
screens.ask: GCF word problem: what is the greatest number of teams?
screens.why:
The number of teams must divide 14 and also 21.
Factors of 14: 1, 2, 7, 14. Factors of 21: 1, 3, 7, 21.
Common factors: 1 and 7. The greatest is 7.
So 7 teams, each with 14 ÷ 7 = 2 girls and 21 ÷ 7 = 3 boys.
(14 teams fails: 21 boys cannot be shared into 14 equal groups.)
screens.clue: The number of teams must divide 14 and also divide 21.

items.why:
Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.
Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18.
Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 6.
The greatest is 6. So GCF(12, 18) = 6.
items.clue: List the factors of 12, then of 18.
Both are powers of 2 times something.

items.ask: Find the GCF of three numbers: GCF(45, 63, 99) = ___
items.why:
45 = 3² × 5.
63 = 3² × 7.
99 = 3² × 11.
All three share only 3², and 3² = 9.
So GCF(45, 63, 99) = 9.
items.clue: Factorize each number. Which prime power do all three share?

test.text: Find the GCF: what is GCF(24, 36)?
test.why:
24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3².
Take each shared prime with the smaller power: 2² and 3.
2² × 3 = 12.
Check: 24 ÷ 12 = 2, 36 ÷ 12 = 3.
So GCF(24, 36) = 12. (72 is a common multiple, not a factor.)

test.ask: GCF word problem: strings of 78 cm, 117 cm and 351 cm are cut into equal pieces with none left over. The longest piece is ___ cm.
test.why:
The piece length must divide 78, 117 and 351.
78 = 2 × 3 × 13, 117 = 3² × 13, 351 = 3³ × 13.
Shared by all three: 3 × 13 = 39.
So the longest piece is 39 cm. (78 = 2 × 39, 117 = 3 × 39, 351 = 9 × 39.)

test.text: Relatively prime: GCF(8, 15) = 1, so 8 and 15 share no prime factor.
test.why:
8 = 2 × 2 × 2.
15 = 3 × 5.
No prime appears in both lists.
So GCF = 1: 8 and 15 are relatively prime. True.

notes.text: The whiteboard problem is Example 2 in section 1.5 of the book, used here as the hook for 1.1.4.

screens.title: Break a number into primes
screens.text: A prime has only two factors: 1 and itself. Keep dividing by the smallest prime that works.
steps: 3 ÷ 3 = 1. Write down the last 3. Stop at 1.

screens.title: Your turn
screens.text: Prime factorization: which is the prime factorization of 20?
screens.why:
20 ÷ 2 = 10.
10 ÷ 2 = 5, and 5 is prime.
So 20 = 2 × 2 × 5.
4 × 5 and 2 × 10 are not finished: 4 and 10 are not prime.
screens.clue: Every factor must be prime. 4 and 10 are not prime.
